newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's BHP seen putting the worst behind it.
newsitem.headline: Australia's BHP seen putting the worst behind it.

text.p: Australia's biggest listed company, The Broken Hill Pty Co (BHP), is expected on Friday to announce its return to annual profit growth and mark the end of a painful earnings rut.
The steel-making, mining and petroleum group is forecast, on average, to report a six percent rise in net profit before abnormals to around A$1.375 billion for the year ended May 31.
Such a result would partly erase a 20 percent profit slump in 1995/96, but would remain a far cry from the rapid growth investors once counted on from the "Big Australian".
Share analysts have forecast BHP to report pre-abnormal net profit of around A$1.35 billion to A$1.4 billion, helped by a late surge in copper production and the world copper price.
"The copper price has been a great performer (in recent months)," fund manager Warren Edney, of Colonial Investment Management, told Reuters on Thursday.
The spot copper price has weakened in recent days, and the futures price suggests further falls.
BHP shares, which make up nine percent of the local market's main All Ordinaries Index, have suffered this week at the hands of the bearish outlook for copper.
But they are still trading at over A$19, well above the depths they plumbed in late 1996 when they sank beneath A$16.
The one-time market darling has been savaged at times, as it comes to grips with underperforming assets, an elusive bull market for commodities and the profit impact of low inflation.
Only last month, investors went on a selling spree after BHP warned of flat earnings until late calendar 1998 and said trading conditions remained tough. Profit forecasts tumbled.
One analyst said he felt BHP's incoming chairman, Jerry Ellis, was trying to puncture inflated hopes for the company.
"They have pitched the expectations at a very low level," said the analyst, who works for a major fund manager.
"I find it hard to believe things are as bad as they have painted."
"Recent developments are going to add to that upside surprise (in 1996/97)," he added, citing a weaker Australian dollar and the May rally in copper prices.

BHP's businesses encompass copper, coal, iron ore, crude oil, liquefied natural gas and steel, but it has been criticised for relying too heavily on a few world-class assets, like the low-cost Escondida copper mine in Chile and its gas operations.
A brokerage report late last year said more than two-thirds of its assets, including its newly acquired Magma copper operations in North America, were underperforming.
BHP has said it will take more asset write-downs as abnormal losses in 1996/97, but analysts were at a loss to predict them.
Analysts are focusing instead on the group's earnings growth from new projects, which are needed to offset long-term weakness in the copper price.
BHP has said major new projects should start to make an impact on its bottom line from late 1998.
